draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the cited studies, several regeneration approaches for PFAS-loaded ion-exchange resins and their limitations are described.

For PS-DVB anion-exchange resins used in drinking-water treatment, Liu and Sun evaluated chloride-based brines as regenerants. They note that, because “using high percentages of organic solvents is challenging in full-scale water treatment, using 10% simple chloride salts without organic solvents might be the most reasonable option for regenerating PFAS-loaded PS-DVB resins.” In their tests on five PS-DVB resins (including macroporous and gel-type materials), regeneration with 10% chloride brine (NH4Cl for A592E, PFA694E, TAN1; NaCl for DOWEX1, IRA910) was identified as the optimal salt condition they examined. Comparison of different anions showed that “chloride salts worked the best for our five tested PS-DVB resins, followed by bicarbonate and … acetate salts,” and they conclude that bicarbonate, though more eco‑friendly and effective for nitrate-laden resins, “is not suitable for PFAS treatment by PS-DVB resins.” Their data also show that cation identity affects performance: “Comparing regeneration with NaCl and NH4Cl … our results also demonstrate that cations could influence the PFAS recovery from IX resins. For example, NH4+ works slightly better for TAN1, while Na+ …” Finally, they assessed pH and NaOH addition by partially replacing NH4Cl or NaCl with NaOH, and observed that “our results indicate that NaOH is a weaker regenerant than NH4Cl or NaCl to recover PFAS.”

Despite optimizing brine composition in this way, regeneration performance was limited. Using 10% brine, “The two gel-type resins, PFA694E and DOWEX1, show < 50% recovery for almost all PFAS, especially for the PFAS-specific PFA694E, which had the lowest recovery (< 25%).” Macroporous resins IRA910 and TAN1 performed better (“IRA910 showed the greatest regeneration recovery among the tested five resins, followed by TAN1”), but chain length remained critical: “When the NCF is above 6, less than 50% recovery was achieved regardless of the PFAS and resin types, whereas PFAS with shorter chain length had significantly higher recovery.” The authors conclude that “resin regeneration for drinking water treatment might be limited for most PFAS except short-chain PFCA and PFECA,” and they classify PFAS-specific resins as essentially non-regenerable by standard methods: “the PFAS-specific resins are non-regenerable in our study via the conventional regeneration approaches, consistent with the manufacturer’s recommendation of one-time use.”

Recognizing that “simple salt solutions do not effectively release PFAS from resins, and it is not practical to regenerate resins every cycle with organic solvents,” Liu and Sun propose an operational compromise. They suggest that “a more practical operation is to regenerate resins with simple salt solutions to release other components in water (major anions, natural organic matter) adsorbed together with PFAS to release these sites for PFAS uptake in the following round of application.” After “multiple cycles when the PFAS-uptake capacity diminishes, it can be determined if it is more feasible to use organic solvents to completely restore the resin capacity for continuous use, or dispose of the exhausted resins at that point.” Thus, in their view, simple brines would mainly clear competing anions and natural organic matter between cycles, whereas organic-solvent regeneration, if used, would be applied infrequently.

At a more general level, Aumeier et al. synthesize regeneration principles for anion exchange resins used for PFAS and related mobile organic contaminants. They note that “for contaminants and anion exchange resins which dominantly interact via electrostatic interactions, regeneration by inorganic salts and/or alkaline solutions is efficient,” while “high-performance anion exchange resins that interact with organic anions such as perfluorooctanoic acid by a combination of hydrophobic effects and electrostatic interaction require organic solvents such as methanol or mixed solvent and salt solutions for desorption.” This highlights that purely electrostatic systems can often be regenerated with simple brines or alkaline solutions, whereas strongly hydrophobic–electrostatic PFAS binding (e.g., PFOA on high-performance resins) necessitates organic-solvent-containing regenerants.

Within this framework, Riegel et al. (as summarized by Aumeier) report an explicit organic-solvent regeneration protocol: “could elute a wide range of PFAS from a loaded anion exchange resin using mixtures of ethanol and NaOH or HCl, reaching satisfactory desorption with only 3 to 10 bed volumes of regeneration solution.” Economically, “after only 2 to 5 regeneration cycles, ion exchange resin could outcompete single-use granular AC cost-wise.” However, these advantages are tempered by operational constraints: “due to the challenges in preventing solvent leaching during reuse and increased efforts for solvent/brine treatment such resins are mainly used in a single-use-and-dispose mode in water treatment so far.” More broadly, Sanzana et al. remark that “although aqueous or solvent-based techniques can be used to regenerate some resins, the waste streams produced are dangerous, expensive to handle, and often incompatible with the treatment processes that produced them,” underscoring the waste-management challenges associated with both aqueous and solvent-based regeneration.

Additional limitations and knowledge gaps are identified at the technology level. Aumeier et al. state that “while anion exchange resins have advantages compared to AC in terms of removal performance of short-chain PFAS anions, knowledge gaps exist in the optimal selection of resins in terms of minimizing negative impact and fouling by natural organic matter as well as regeneration options.” Coupled with Sanzana et al.’s statement that waste streams from aqueous or solvent-based regeneration “are dangerous, expensive to handle, and often incompatible” with the originating processes, this indicates that resin choice, fouling behavior, and downstream handling of regenerant waste are still significant open questions for practical deployment.

Beyond salts and conventional solvents, several alternative or novel regeneration strategies are discussed. Liu and Sun note that “activated-persulfate oxidation is a promising in-situ regeneration method for degrading PFCA,” and also refer to work where “higher PFAS removal [was observed] using resins in sulfate forms than in chloride forms.” They explicitly caution, however, that “These studies used regenerable resins, while it is unclear whether the same approaches could regenerate PFAS-specific resins,” and they emphasize again that PFAS-specific resins were non-regenerable under the conventional conditions they tested.

Another approach uses surfactant-assisted desorption combined with destructive treatment of the desorption stream. Zheng et al. report that “cationic cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) enabled the efficient desorption of PFOS from saturated ion-exchange resins (IERs), providing a practical regeneration strategy.” Mechanistically, CTAB “displaces PFOS from IERs owing to its stronger hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions with the resin.” Importantly for reuse, “The regenerated IERs retained their adsorption efficiency over at least five reuse cycles.” The concentrated desorption stream was then directly treated: “The concentrated PFOS–CTAB eluent was fed directly into a UV/SO3²⁻ process, achieving approximately 99.9% PFOS degradation and 90.3% defluorination.” This illustrates an integrated capture–regeneration–destruction scheme, in which CTAB regeneration maintains resin performance over multiple cycles and UV/sulfite treatment manages the PFOS-containing regenerant.

In the available membrane PFAS studies, one key limitation for cross-study comparison is that some work uses natural raw water while many other studies do not. In the natural raw water study, the authors explicitly state that, “Other studies have not used natural raw water as was done in this study, which hampers direct comparisons.” This means that the raw water matrix itself differs from the simpler or synthetic matrices used elsewhere, so differences in PFAS removal cannot be attributed solely to membrane properties.

A second complicating feature of natural or real-world matrices is the presence of many other contaminants. In a study on PFAS removal from real wastewater, the matrix contained “pollutants that compete for adsorption or rejection by the membrane,” and “This competition can reduce the efficiency of the membrane for PFAS removal compared to simpler matrices.” Thus, in complex natural or wastewater matrices, multiple co-pollutants vie for the same adsorption or rejection sites, so observed PFAS removals can be lower than in cleaner, simpler feed waters, making direct comparison across matrices uncertain.

The behavior of small PFAS adds further complexity in natural raw water. In one study, “PFASs with molecular weights (MWs) lower than the nominal MWCO of 270 Da were found to be concentrated by the membrane process by a factor of approximately two,” and “This indicates that other processes than size exclusion were involved for the rejection of PFASs, such as electrostatic repulsion and diffusion into the polymeric phase of the membrane.” Because small PFAS with MW below the nominal MWCO did not simply pass through but were concentrated and rejected via additional mechanisms, it becomes difficult to compare their removal between natural raw water experiments and studies using simpler matrices where such effects may differ. These findings should be interpreted as study-specific limitations on comparability, not as universal rules for all membranes, PFAS, or water types.
